prompt.context: Your client is Yoga Jones, the owner of Orange Yoga Studio. Orange Yoga is a very popular, up-scale yoga studio in New York City known for high quality instruction and a relaxed vibe. Yoga Jones has owned and operated Orange Yoga for the past 5 years. For its first four years, Orange Yoga was very financially successful; however in the past year, Yoga Jones noticed that her profits seem to be declining. She doesn't keep very good financial records and has made a few big investments lately, so is having a hard time figuring out a) whether she is actually losing profit and b) how to fix her financial woes.
prompt.question: How do you help Yoga Jones?

clarifying_info.q: What types of classes does Orange Yoga offer and how many per day?
clarifying_info.a: Orange Yoga offers 5 classes daily on weekdays and 4 classes on weekends. All classes are 'Vinyasa Flow' style.
Clients pay on a per-class basis. There are currently no package deals or membership rates.
The competitive landscape for yoga studios in NYC has remained unchanged over the past three years.
Yoga Jones made major maintenance upgrades: installing hardwood floors, fresh paint, and new shower facilities. These were financed primarily through loans.

All costs are fixed (no variable costs per customer). Five main fixed costs: Rent/utilities = $3,500/month; Liability Insurance = $1,800/year; Administration costs (owner salary, supplies, computer, marketing) = $800/week; Yoga instructor salaries = $50/class; Loan payments = $500/month.

Class fees are the only source of revenue. All classes cost $12. Average of 8 students per class on weekdays and 6 students per class on weekends. Assume every month has 22 weekdays and 8 weekend days.

exhibits.title: Average number of weekday students in Orange Yoga classes
exhibits.shows: Two charts: (1) a bar chart showing average number of weekday students per class time slot in 2014 across five time slots (7am, 10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm); (2) a line chart showing average number of weekday students by class time slot over years 2010-2014 for the same five time slots.
exhibits.data: Y-axis ranges 0-12 students; five time slots shown: 7am, 10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm; data covers 2010-2014 trend and 2014 snapshot

exhibits.title: Average number of weekend students in Orange Yoga classes
exhibits.shows: Two charts: (1) a bar chart showing average number of weekend students per class time slot in 2014 across four time slots (10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm); (2) a line chart showing average number of weekend students by class time slot over years 2010-2014 for the same four time slots.
exhibits.data: Y-axis ranges 0-12 students; four time slots shown: 10am, 12pm, 6pm, 8pm; data covers 2010-2014 trend and 2014 snapshot

framework: Revenue = Price per class × Number of students per class × Number of classes
Cost breakdown: Rent, Insurance, Instructor salaries, Admin costs, Loan payments
Identify whether profit is positive or negative
Diagnose root cause of decline (cost increases vs. revenue decline)
Brainstorm levers: revenue enhancement and cost reduction
Evaluate feasibility of changes (class restructuring, capacity expansion)

questions.prompt: Calculate monthly revenue for Orange Yoga.
questions.guidance: Candidate should separate weekday and weekend revenue. Weekday: $12 × 5 classes/day × 8 students/class × 22 days = $10,560. Weekend: $12 × 4 classes/day × 6 students/class × 8 days = $2,304. Total = $12,864/month.

math.setup: Revenue = price × classes/day × students/class × days/month, calculated separately for weekdays and weekends

questions.prompt: Calculate monthly costs for Orange Yoga.
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert all costs to monthly basis: Insurance = $1,800/12 = $150/month; Admin = $800 × 4 = $3,200/month (using 4 weeks); Weekday instructor salaries = $50 × 5 × 22 = $5,500/month; Weekend instructor salaries = $50 × 4 × 8 = $1,600/month. Sum all five cost categories.

math.setup: Convert all costs to monthly: Rent ($3,500), Insurance ($1,800/12), Admin ($800/week × 4 weeks), Instructor salaries (weekday + weekend), Loan payments ($500)

questions.prompt: Is Orange Yoga currently profitable? By how much?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute Profit = Revenue - Costs = $12,864 - $14,450 = -$1,586 (approx. -$1.6K to -$1.7K). The studio is losing roughly $1,650/month. Candidate should note the loss is driven by the rent increase ($2,000/month) and teacher salary raise ($10/class) that occurred last year.

math.setup: Profit = Total Monthly Revenue - Total Monthly Costs

questions.prompt: Analyze the exhibit data on student attendance by class time. What patterns do you see and what are the implications?
questions.guidance: Weekday insights: midday classes (10am, 12pm) have fewer students than morning (7am) and evening (6pm, 8pm) classes; this trend has grown more pronounced over 5 years; notably the 10am class likely does not cover teacher salary ($50) at its attendance level. Weekend insights: opposite profile - midday classes (10am, 12pm) are most popular; evening classes (6pm, 8pm) are much less popular; 6pm and 8pm weekend classes likely do not cover teacher salary. Strong candidates will note the max average attendance peaks at 10 students for both weekday and weekend, suggesting capacity is being hit at peak times. Strong candidates will hypothesize restructuring class times, eliminating unprofitable classes, and adding classes during high-demand slots.

math.setup: Teacher salary breakeven: at $50/class and $12/student, need at least ceil(50/12) = 5 students to cover instructor cost
steps: Breakeven students per class = $50 / $12 = 4.17, so minimum 5 students needed to cover instructor
Weekday 10am class appears to have fewer than 5 students in recent years
Weekend 6pm and 8pm classes appear to have fewer than 5 students in recent years
math.answer: Weekday 10am and weekend 6pm/8pm classes do not cover teacher salary and should be candidates for elimination

questions.prompt: Yoga Jones' studio is 13ft long and 21ft wide. The average yoga mat is 6ft long and 2ft wide. Minimum distance between two mats is 1 foot, and minimum distance between a mat and a wall is 6 inches. How many mats can she fit?
questions.guidance: Each mat effectively requires a 7ft × 3ft footprint (6ft mat + 1ft gap on one end = 7ft; 2ft mat + 1ft gap on one side = 3ft) after accounting for spacing. Alternatively, each mat needs 21 sq ft. Studio area = 13 × 21 = 273 sq ft. 273 / 21 = 13 mats. The instructor does not need a mat. Candidates can also draw it out to arrive at 13.

math.setup: Method 1 (area): effective mat area = (6ft + 1ft spacing) × (2ft + 1ft spacing) = 7 × 3 = 21 sq ft; Studio area = 13 × 21 = 273 sq ft. Method 2 (drawing layout): arrange mats in rows accounting for 6-inch wall buffer and 1-foot inter-mat gap.
steps: Studio area = 13 ft × 21 ft = 273 sq ft
Effective area per mat = 7 ft × 3 ft = 21 sq ft
math.answer: 13 mats (instructor does not need a mat)

questions.prompt: If Yoga Jones eliminates all classes that do not cover teacher salary and begins allowing 13 students per class (assume all classes currently at 10 students have a waiting list of at least 3 students), will this save the studio? Calculate the new profit.
questions.guidance: Eliminate: 1 weekday class (10am) and 2 weekend classes (6pm and 8pm). New weekday schedule: 4 classes per day — 3 classes with 13 students, 1 class with 5 students (the remaining lower-attendance class). New weekend schedule: 2 classes per day — both with 13 students. Recalculate revenue and instructor salaries accordingly. All other costs unchanged.

math.setup: New revenue: weekday (3 classes × 13 students + 1 class × 5 students) × $12 × 22 days; weekend (2 classes × 13 students) × $12 × 8 days. New instructor salary: weekday $50 × 4 classes × 22 days; weekend $50 × 2 classes × 8 days.
steps: Total new costs = $7,350 + $4,400 + $800 = $12,550 (note: casebook shows $12,500 — minor rounding)
math.answer: Approximately +$1,612/month profit (casebook rounds to ~$1.6K) — the studio moves from a $1.6K/month loss to a $1.6K/month profit

brainstorming.prompt: After analyzing her books, Yoga Jones realizes that her decline in profit began after a $2,000/month rent increase last year and a decision to raise all teacher salaries by $10/class. She does not want to move and believes strongly in paying her teachers a high wage. What else can she do?

categories.name: Revenue: Pricing
ideas: Implement variable pricing (charge more for peak classes or premium slots)
Introduce surge pricing for high-demand evening/morning classes

categories.name: Revenue: Product/Service Diversification
ideas: Offer higher-priced specialty classes (e.g., pilates, hot yoga)
Start private classes or one-on-one instruction at premium rates
Sell related products: yoga mats, water bottles, apparel
Offer class packages or memberships at a slight discount to improve retention and predictability

categories.name: Revenue: Volume
ideas: Offer more classes, especially at high-demand times
Market to attract more students to under-attended classes
Partner with corporate wellness programs to drive group bookings

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Eliminate unprofitable classes (those not covering teacher salary)
Negotiate lower rent or sublease unused studio time
Explore refinancing loans at lower interest rate (though loan payments are relatively small — limited upside)

recommendation: Orange Yoga is currently losing approximately $1,600/month due primarily to a $2,000/month rent increase and teacher salary raises last year

Recommend two immediate actions: (1) eliminate the 3 unprofitable classes (weekday 10am, weekend 6pm, weekend 8pm) that do not cover instructor cost, and (2) increase maximum class size from 10 to 13 students (supported by studio floor space calculation and existing waiting lists)
These two changes together convert the studio from a ~$1,600/month loss to a ~$1,600/month profit
risks: Long-term clients who valued flexible class times may churn when their preferred time slot is eliminated
Clients who valued the intimate small-class experience may be dissatisfied with larger classes (10 → 13 students)
Instructors whose classes are eliminated may feel demoralized or leave, which could impact quality and reputation
Increasing class size without proportional improvement in studio layout could reduce the 'relaxed vibe' differentiator
next_steps: Communicate changes proactively to clients; offer transitional incentives (e.g., a free class) to those whose time slots are affected
Explore further revenue diversification: raise prices, introduce packages/memberships, add specialty or private classes
Evaluate adding more classes during peak demand times (evenings on weekdays, mornings on weekends) to capture waiting-list demand
Revisit financial tracking processes so Yoga Jones can monitor profitability in real time going forward
